paras: The lynching of Jake Hines was the fatal whipping of a young Black man, named in the papers as Jake Hines or Jake Haines, by a band of white men near Young's Island in Colleton County, South Carolina, in February 1903. Suspected of stealing hogs or meat from a neighbor, he was taken from his house and flogged, and he died of his wounds several days later. South Carolina weeklies and papers in Georgia, Florida and Arkansas carried the story under headlines about "whitecaps," and a Columbia dispatch noted that the local magistrate was himself in jail on a murder charge. The Colored American reported it as a killing "on the mere suspicion of stealing."

Hines was described as "a young negro man" who lived on Young's Island, which the Columbia dispatch placed "near Charleston" and the Lexington Dispatch placed in Colleton county. He was suspected of stealing from a neighbor: the Columbia dispatch said hogs, while the Walterboro correspondent of The State said "some meat from one of the neighbors."

According to the Walterboro dispatch, a crowd of "about 10 or 12 white men" came to his house several nights before February 12. The men found no meat, but under his bed they found what the Columbia dispatch called "a bag of fertilizer" and the Walterboro dispatch "three sacks of guano." Hines was taken out and beaten until he collapsed, and the Columbia account said the beating "was long continued" because he would not say whether he had accomplices.

The Walterboro version gave a different sequence: Hines refused to confess but named another Black man, who "proved himself innocent to the satisfaction of the men." The crowd then took Hines into the woods and beat him again. He died of his wounds on February 11 or 12, depending on the account.

The Walterboro dispatch, dated February 12, said a coroner's inquest would be held that day and that no arrests had yet been made. According to the Columbia dispatch, no magistrate could investigate, because Magistrate L. C. Behling, who had jurisdiction, had killed a neighbor in a land dispute and was in the Walterboro jail. No report of the inquest's finding, of any arrest, or of a prosecution appears in the coverage.

Two separate reports dated February 12 carried the story: a Columbia dispatch, run by the Savannah Morning News the next day as "Hog Thief Whipped Now He Is Dead," and a Walterboro report to The State that South Carolina weeklies reprinted the following week. Redated Charleston, February 13, the Columbia text appeared in the Americus Times-Recorder and the Ocala Banner as "Inhuman Work of Whitecaps," and in the Keowee Courier and the Bamberg Herald. The Forrest City Times in Arkansas reduced it to a single sentence. The Walterboro text ran in the Newberry Herald and News, the Lancaster Ledger, the Watchman and Southron of Sumter and, a second time, in the Bamberg Herald, under headlines such as "Whitecaps Whip Negro to Death."

Most white papers printed the dispatches without comment, though the Savannah headline called Hines a "hog thief" whom its text called only a suspect. The Lexington Dispatch paraphrased the story in its editorial column, calling Hines "a young negro buck," and closed the item with the line "The way of the transgressor is hard and the road thereof leads to death."

The only Black-press report in the coverage was a brief in the Colored American's "Race Gleanings" column on February 21. In contrast to the Lexington editorial, it stressed that "no attempt was made to fasten the crime on him," remarked "Fine community of Christians, indeed," and pointed out that the local magistrate was in jail for killing a white neighbor.

The two dispatches differ on the date of death: the Columbia report said Hines died the morning of February 12, which the Bamberg Herald's version gave as "Thursday morning," while the Walterboro report, of the same date, said he died "yesterday." They also differ on the property, hogs or meat, and on what was found, a bag of fertilizer or three sacks of guano. The Walterboro dispatch came from the county seat and is the only account to give the size of the crowd.

reader.title: Lynching of Jake Hines
bases: A band of 10 or 12 white men called whitecappers whipped a Black man suspected of theft, and he died of the wounds [A1, A7].
Hines died of a whipping by about 10 or 12 white men acting without legal authority [A1, A7], who punished him on suspicion of stealing hogs or meat [A1, A7].

Two independent dispatches, from Columbia [A1] and from Walterboro to The State [A7], agree that whitecappers whipped Hines to death on suspicion of theft, and the Colored American confirms the flogging death [A13].

accounts.label: Columbia wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A party of whitecappers searched Hines's house for stolen hogs, found only fertilizer, and beat him until he collapsed, prolonging the beating because he would not name accomplices; he died the morning of Feb. 12, and no magistrate could investigate.

accounts.label: Walterboro correspondent (The State)
accounts.gist: About 10 or 12 white men whipped him on suspicion of stealing a neighbor's meat, found three sacks of guano, took him into the woods and beat him again after the man he named was cleared; he died Feb. 11; an inquest was set and no arrests made.

accounts.label: Black weekly
accounts.gist: Jake Haines was 'brutally flogged to death' in Colleton county on 'the mere suspicion of stealing', with no attempt to fasten the crime on him.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Whipped Negro to Death', 'Inhuman Work of Whitecaps', 'Whitecaps Whip Negro to Death' over unremarked dispatch text.
Savannah Morning News headlined 'Hog Thief Whipped Now He Is Dead' though its text said only that he was suspected, and stressed the 'peculiar situation' of the jailed magistrate.
Lexington Dispatch called him 'a young negro buck' and closed with 'The way of the transgressor is hard and the road thereof leads to death.'
Colored American: 'brutally flogged to death' on 'the mere suspicion of stealing'; 'Fine community of Christians, indeed.'
